title: Collateral Adverse Outcomes in Orthopaedic Surgery.
authors: Nguyen KT, Yamanouchi K, Bansal A, Daniels AH, Louie PK
abstract:
1. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2026 Nov 17. doi: 10.2106/JBJS.26.00479. Online ahead of
 print.

Collateral Adverse Outcomes in Orthopaedic Surgery.

Nguyen KT(1)(2), Yamanouchi K(1)(3), Bansal A(1), Daniels AH(4), Louie PK(1).



➢ Collateral adverse outcomes (CAOs) are expected, procedure-inherent sequelae 
of technically sound surgery that represent accepted trade-offs rather than 
failures of care. They must be distinguished from true postoperative 
complications and also from injury-related sequelae and the natural history of 
the underlying disease, which arise independent of a correctly performed 
operation.➢ A CAO is defined by 4 criteria: (1) it is mechanistically inherent 
to the procedure, (2) it is predictable at a procedure-specific frequency, (3) 
its frequency and severity can be reduced but cannot be eliminated through use 
of a standard technique, and (4) it is within an expected severity range. An 
outcome that exceeds this severity range, requires escalation of care, or arises 
primarily from a technical error or an inappropriate indication is a 
complication rather than a CAO.➢ CAOs occur across all orthopaedic 
subspecialties and are driven by the biomechanical, anatomic, and biologic 
requirements of each procedure; common examples include dysphagia after anterior 
cervical spine surgery, donor-site morbidity after anterior cruciate ligament 
reconstruction, and kneeling difficulty after total knee arthroplasty.➢ 
Preoperative counseling is the most effective and universally applicable 
management strategy, as accurate expectations reduce unnecessary concern and 
support shared decision-making; because patients do not always experience a 
high-incidence CAO as distinct from a complication, the distinction should be 
communicated in patient-centered terms rather than used to declare an outcome 
acceptable on the patient's behalf.➢ Where possible, CAOs should be reduced in 
frequency and severity, although they cannot be eliminated, through 
evidence-based technical modifications, including perioperative corticosteroids 
for dysphagia, oblique harvest incisions to reduce saphenous nerve injury, and 
minimally invasive approaches to limit paraspinal atrophy.➢ CAOs should be 
recorded separately within outcome registries and consent processes, with their 
severity and any need for treatment captured rather than excluded from 
reporting.

title: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's professional football: Higher incidence and distinct injury patterns compared to men.
authors: Huber L, Krutsch W, Memmel C, Weber J, Alt V, Szymski D
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 17. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70692.
Online  ahead of print.

Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's professional football: Higher 
incidence and distinct injury patterns compared to men.

Huber L(1)(2), Krutsch W(1)(2)(3), Memmel C(2)(4), Weber J(1)(2), Alt V(1)(2), 
Szymski D(1)(2).



PURPOSE: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are more frequent in female 
football players, but sex-specific differences in injury characteristics remain 
insufficiently understood. This study aimed to analyse sex-specific differences 
in ACL injury incidence and characteristics in professional football.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study used data from a German national ACL 
registry ('Kreuzbandregister im Deutschen Fußball'), including professional male 
(first to third league) and female (first and second league) football players 
from the 2016/2017 to 2024/2025 seasons. Incidence rates were compared using 
Poisson regression (incidence rate ratio, IRR) and injury characteristics using 
multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: A total of 459 ACL injuries were analysed (177 female and 282 male). 
The rate was 1.19 versus 0.69 per 1000 match hours (IRR 1.69, 95% confidence 
interval [CI] 1.34-2.13). The difference was most pronounced in the first 
division (IRR 2.49, 1.82-3.41) and smaller and not significant in the lower 
leagues (IRR 1.24, 0.93-1.65). Injuries in female players were more often 
non-contact (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.37) and indirect-contact injuries (aOR 
2.92), occurred more often on artificial turf (aOR 5.42) and in national team 
players (aOR 3.03). Concomitant injury patterns did not differ significantly, 
except for fewer lateral collateral ligament injuries in women.
CONCLUSION: ACL injury rates are higher in female professional football players, 
particularly in the first division. The predominance of non-contact and 
indirect-contact mechanisms supports targeted, sex-specific prevention 
strategies.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, prospective cohort study.

title: Facility Cost Differences Between Single-stage and Two-stage Exchange for Chronic Periprosthetic Joint Infection: A Time-driven Activity-based Costing Analysis.
authors: Lam AD, Sutton RM, Lizcano JD, Sherman MB, Brown S, Courtney PM, Krueger CA
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3305-e3311. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01024. Epub 2026 Jun 18.

Facility Cost Differences Between Single-stage and Two-stage Exchange for 
Chronic Periprosthetic Joint Infection: A Time-driven Activity-based Costing 
Analysis.

Lam AD(1), Sutton RM, Lizcano JD, Sherman MB, Brown S, Courtney PM, Krueger CA.



BACKGROUND: With increasing data supporting the use of single-stage exchange 
over two-stage exchange for select patients with periprosthetic joint infection 
(PJI) after total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA), it 
is important to specifically quantify cost differences between the two 
procedures. This study aimed to compare itemized facility costs of single-stage 
and two-stage exchange.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study identified 118 consecutive patients who 
were diagnosed with chronic PJI and underwent revision THA or TKA at a single 
high-volume academic institution. Of 63 hip PJI patients (53.4%), 38 (60.3%) 
underwent single-stage revision and 25 (39.7%) underwent two-stage revision. 
From 55 knee PJI patients (46.6%), 19 (34.5%) underwent single-stage revision 
and 36 (65.5%) underwent two-stage exchange. Patients were excluded if they had 
soft-tissue coverage requirements or extensive bone loss requiring 
endoprosthesis. Facility costs were calculated using time-driven activity-based 
costing methodology. Costs were combined for the two hospital admissions for a 
two-stage exchange.
RESULTS: Patients undergoing single-stage revision TKA had lower personnel 
($46,397 vs. $78,765, P < 0.001), implant ($19,822 vs. $85,605, P < 0.001), and 
overall costs ($79,548 vs. $171,592, P < 0.001) when compared with two-stage 
revision. Similarly, patients undergoing single-stage revision THA had lower 
personnel ($46,718 vs. 99,255, P < 0.001), implant ($19,936 vs. 73,372, P < 
0.001), and overall costs ($79,349 vs. 187,251, P < 0.001) than two-staged 
procedures. Implant costs demonstrated the highest variation between two-stage 
and one-stage revisions for TKA (4.3 times) and THA (3.7 times). Total surgical 
time was significantly longer in two-staged THA (365 vs. 175 minutes, P < 0.001) 
and TKA (256 vs. 162 minutes, P < 0.001) revisions.
CONCLUSION: Single-staged revisions cost markedly less than two-staged 
procedures for first-time, chronic PJI when using strict surgical indications. 
Given the growing emphasis on value-based care, if single-stage arthroplasty is 
at least as effective as two-stage exchange in some PJI settings, the cost 
savings of this procedure would be tremendous.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Impact of an Orthopaedic-Driven Perioperative Protocol to Optimize Social and Medical Risk (SAFE) following Elective Total Joint Arthroplasty in a Health Safety-Net Hospital.
authors: Abdeen A, Olszewski N, Bemis K, Kain MS, Freccero DM, Tornetta P 3rd
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3284-e3292. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01301. Epub 2026 May 13.

Impact of an Orthopaedic-Driven Perioperative Protocol to Optimize Social and 
Medical Risk (SAFE) following Elective Total Joint Arthroplasty in a Health 
Safety-Net Hospital.

Abdeen A(1), Olszewski N, Bemis K, Kain MS, Freccero DM, Tornetta P 3rd.



BACKGROUND: Preoperative optimization of medical risk factors before total joint 
arthroplasty of the hip and knee improves outcomes. Arthroplasty programs in 
health safety-net hospitals have increased risk of complications because of 
increased medical complexity and disparities of social determinants of health. 
We propose a novel, orthopaedic team-driven perioperative optimization protocol 
to comprehensively and systematically address medical and social risk factors 
before total joint arthroplasty. We aim to evaluate the effect of optimizing 
medical and social risk factors on outcomes after hip and knee arthroplasty in a 
health safety-net hospital.
METHODS: A retrospective case-control series was done in a single, academic, 
tertiary-care, urban, safety-net hospital to compare complications (primary 
outcome) readmissions, length of stay (LOS), discharge disposition and 
escalation of care to intensive care unit (ICU), revision surgeries, and 
mortality (secondary outcomes) in patients who underwent hip or knee 
arthroplasty by a single surgeon before and after implementation of the 
optimization protocol. Follow-up duration was 12 months. Social determinants of 
health (SDOH) burden between groups were compared.
RESULTS: Of 808 primary total joint arthroplasty patients, 409 had surgery after 
the optimization protocol was implemented and 399 control subjects had surgery 
before implementation. Study patients had lower 90-day deep infection rate 
(0.24% vs 1%; P = 0.017) and 1-year deep infection rate (0.24 vs 2.01%; P = 
0.017) compared with control subjects, respectively. Study patients versus 
control subjects: LOS (3.0 vs 3.5 days, P = 0.012), discharge to skilled nursing 
facility (SNF) (11.0 vs 17.0%, P = 0.015), escalation to ICU care (0.25 vs 2.5%, 
P = 0.006), and 1-year mortality (0.24 vs 2.5%, P = 0.074), respectively. SDOH 
burden was similar between control and study groups.
CONCLUSION: Implementation of an orthopaedic-driven, standardized protocol 
designed to address modifiable medical and social risk factors before elective 
primary hip and knee arthroplasty was associated with reduced infection, LOS, 
discharge to SNF, and escalation of ICU care in a health safety-net hospital.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Mid-term outcomes of medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction using suture tape in paediatric and adolescent population: a case series.
authors: Youssef K, Vampertzis T, Gangadharan R, Rad D, Bailey M, Wadia F
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Nov 19;64:104686. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104686. Online ahead of 
print.

Mid-term outcomes of medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction using suture 
tape in paediatric and adolescent population: a case series.

Youssef K(1), Vampertzis T(2), Gangadharan R(3), Rad D(3), Bailey M(3), Wadia 
F(3).



BACKGROUND: Suture tape medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) reconstruction 
avoids tendon graft harvest, but outcomes in children are poorly reported. This 
study evaluated functional outcomes and complications in children and 
adolescents with recurrent patellar instability.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort of 56 patients (77 knees; 40 female; mean age 
14.3 years, range 8.2-17.7) underwent isolated suture tape MPFL reconstruction 
for recurrent instability at a tertiary centre between 2020 and 2025. Minimum 
follow-up was 6 months. The primary outcome was the Paediatric International 
Knee Documentation Committee (Pedi-IKDC) score at ≥6 months (available for 58 
knees). Secondary outcomes were recurrent instability, extensor lag and other 
complications.
RESULTS: The mean Pedi-IKDC score improved from 49.6 (SD 13.9) to 79.6 (SD 
16.9), a mean gain of 30.0 points (p < 0.001). Recurrent instability occurred in 
5 of 77 knees (6.5%), one following trauma, despite trochlear dysplasia (Dejour 
B-D) in 79% of knees. An extensor lag was recorded in 17 of 65 knees (26.2%): 16 
of these were 5-10° and resolved with physiotherapy within 3-6 months; one of 
approximately 25° is awaiting revision. Steroid injection for medial patellar 
pain was required in four knees (5.2%). No physeal complications were observed.
CONCLUSION: Suture tape MPFL reconstruction improved the Pedi-IKDC score by 30.0 
points, more than three times the minimal clinically important difference, with 
recurrent instability (6.5%) comparable to tendon graft reconstruction in 
children and no physeal complications. Extensor lag (26.2%) was common but 
resolved with physiotherapy in all but one knee. Suture tape is a reasonable 
graft-free option; comparative studies are needed.

title: Ultracongruent inserts are associated with a higher Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement at 18 months than posterior-stabilized inserts after primary total knee arthroplasty: A matched cohort study.
authors: Isla J, Escudero P, Teneo A, Salas H, Aracena J, Sanchez S, Hermosilla H, Castillo M, Gonzalez W
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Nov 18;21:101239. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101239. Online
ahead  of print.

Ultracongruent inserts are associated with a higher Knee Injury and 
Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement at 18 months than 
posterior-stabilized inserts after primary total knee arthroplasty: A matched 
cohort study.

Isla J(1), Escudero P(2), Teneo A(2), Salas H(2), Aracena J(3), Sanchez S(4), 
Hermosilla H(4), Castillo M(4), Gonzalez W(5).



PURPOSE: The purpose of the study is to compare 18-month functional outcomes and 
preoperative-to-postoperative improvement in the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis 
Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS-JR) between ultracongruent (UC) and 
posterior-stabilized (PS) inserts in patients undergoing primary total knee 
arthroplasty (TKA) with posterior cruciate ligament sacrifice using the same 
implant system.
METHODS: This retrospective matched cohort study included patients who underwent 
primary TKA between 2017 and 2022 using the Stryker Triathlon® system. After 
matching, 200 patients were analyzed: 100 treated with UC inserts and 100 with 
PS inserts. Groups were matched by sex, age, body mass index, follow-up 
duration, and Kellgren-Lawrence grade. The primary outcome was KOOS-JR at 18 
months. Preoperative KOOS-JR was recorded to calculate absolute improvement. 
Secondary outcomes included the Knee Society Score knee component (KSS-Knee) and 
the function component (KSS-Function). Multivariable linear regression was 
performed to adjust for potential confounders.
RESULTS: At 18 months, the UC group demonstrated higher KOOS-JR scores than the 
PS group (mean ± standard deviation, 86.1 ± 9.2 vs 70.3 ± 9.2 points; mean 
difference, 15.8 points; 95% confidence interval [CI], 13.2 to 18.4; p < 0.001). 
KSS-Knee and KSS-Function scores also favored UC inserts. In adjusted analyses, 
UC insert use remained associated with higher postoperative KOOS-JR and greater 
KOOS-JR improvement.
CONCLUSION: Patients who received surgeon-selected UC inserts had higher 
18-month functional scores than those who received PS inserts. However, insert 
selection was influenced by surgeon preference and intraoperative assessment, 
and the principal biomechanical determinants of that decision were not available 
for matching or adjustment. The observed association may therefore reflect 
differences in case complexity rather than insert design alone and should not be 
interpreted as evidence of comparative superiority.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: From Priority Questions to Registry-Nested Trials: An AJRR-C Road Map for Advancing Arthroplasty Research.
authors: Bedard NA, Hannon CP, Springer BD, Huddleston JI 3rd, Kremers HM, Lewallen DG, Berry DJ
abstract:
1. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2026 Nov 18. doi: 10.2106/JBJS.26.01407. Online ahead of
 print.

From Priority Questions to Registry-Nested Trials: An AJRR-C Road Map for 
Advancing Arthroplasty Research.

Bedard NA(1), Hannon CP(1), Springer BD(2), Huddleston JI 3rd(3), Kremers HM(1), 
Lewallen DG(1), Berry DJ(1).



BACKGROUND: The American Joint Replacement Research-Collaborative (AJRR-C) is a 
National Institutes of Health-funded P30 Core Center for Clinical Research and 
seeks to accelerate practice-changing arthroplasty research by leveraging the 
American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) and shared multicenter research 
infrastructure. The AJRR-C convened 2 complementary meetings to establish a 
scalable coordinated pathway from the identification of high-priority clinical 
questions to the initiation of prospective studies.
METHODS: In July 2025, leaders from The Hip Society, The Knee Society, the 
American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons, the AJRR, the Orthopaedic 
Research and Education Foundation, and the broader research community identified 
and prioritized clinical research questions regarding infection, perioperative 
management, new technologies, surgical techniques, implants, and quality. In 
April 2026, orthopaedic surgeons, methodologists, and artificial intelligence 
experts reconvened to evaluate contemporary approaches for addressing these 
priorities.
RESULTS: A central theme of the meetings was the importance of utilizing a 
fit-for-purpose approach in which study design is tailored to the clinical 
question, available data, and potential sources of bias. Clinical questions with 
clear equipoise and feasible interventions may warrant randomization, whereas 
questions involving rare outcomes, rapidly evolving technologies, surgeon 
preferences, or long-term surveillance may be better addressed with 
observational studies. Participants emphasized the need for a robust, 
sustainable network for arthroplasty clinical trials that provides the shared 
infrastructure necessary for coordinated site engagement, standardized data 
definitions, reliable longitudinal follow-up, and AJRR linkage across 
multicenter trials. Two new AJRR-nested randomized trials arose from the 
priority-topics meeting, and their development demonstrates the potential of the 
AJRR-C consensus model to translate research priorities into practice-changing 
evidence generation.
CONCLUSIONS: The AJRR-C established a coordinated pathway from the 
prioritization of research to the implementation of multicenter studies to 
address high-priority arthroplasty research questions. Sustaining this model 
requires continued collaboration among orthopaedic societies, investigators, 
methodologists, and the AJRR, as well as reliable funding mechanisms.

title: Bone-patellar tendon-bone and quadriceps tendon autografts are associated with a higher 1-year risk of thigh muscle injury after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in competitive male athletes: A retrospective cohort study.
authors: Pecci J, Kotsifaki R, Getgood A, Whiteley R
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 18. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70695.
Online  ahead of print.

Bone-patellar tendon-bone and quadriceps tendon autografts are associated with a 
higher 1-year risk of thigh muscle injury after anterior cruciate ligament 
reconstruction in competitive male athletes: A retrospective cohort study.

Pecci J(1)(2), Kotsifaki R(2), Getgood A(3)(4), Whiteley R(2).



PURPOSE: To investigate the association between anterior cruciate ligament 
reconstruction (ACLR) graft type and subsequent thigh muscle injury in athletes 
involved in pivoting sports.
METHODS: A retrospective observational study was conducted on 221 ACLRs 
performed in 199 competitive male athletes involved in pivoting sports, 
classified according to graft donor site: extensor mechanism (bone-patellar 
tendon-bone [BPTB] or quadriceps tendon) and flexor mechanism (hamstring 
tendon). Only athletes who returned to sport and completed a minimum of 12 
months of follow-up were included. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed 
thigh muscle injuries occurring within the first year following the discharge 
date were identified and classified by muscle group injured and graft type.
RESULTS: Thirty-five athletes (15.8%) sustained at least one MRI-confirmed thigh 
muscle injury (41 muscle-group-level injuries in total) in the year after 
discharge from ACLR. Athletes who received a graft from the extensor mechanism 
had a higher proportion of any thigh muscle injury than those with hamstring 
grafts (27/133, 20.3% vs. 8/88, 9.1%; absolute risk difference 11.2%, 95% 
confidence interval [CI] 1.4-20.0; odds ratio [OR] 2.45, 95% CI 1.12-5.88; 
p = 0.037). Muscle-group analyses showed no significant differences for 
hamstring injury or quadriceps injury. All six adductor injuries occurred in the 
extensor donor group (4.5% vs. 0%), but this difference was not statistically 
robust. After adjustment, none of the three muscle-group comparisons remained 
significant.
CONCLUSION: Extensor mechanism grafts were associated with a higher proportion 
of athletes sustaining any thigh muscle injury in the year following discharge 
from rehabilitation; although absolute rates were low, no individual muscle 
group showed a significant difference.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Planned extension gap widening is associated with greater intraoperative flexion contracture correction in robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Leal-Blanquet J, Pons-Riverola A, Erquicia JI, Hinarejos P, Torres-Claramunt R, Novillo M, Mojal S, Pujol O
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 18. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70691.
Online  ahead of print.

Planned extension gap widening is associated with greater intraoperative flexion 
contracture correction in robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty.

Leal-Blanquet J(1)(2)(3), Pons-Riverola A(1)(3), Erquicia JI(1)(2), Hinarejos 
P(4), Torres-Claramunt R(4), Novillo M(2), Mojal S(5), Pujol O(2)(3)(6).



PURPOSE: To quantify the effect of posterior capsular release and extension-gap 
widening on intraoperative extension deficit correction during robotic-assisted 
total knee arthroplasty (TKA), and to identify patient-specific factors 
associated with the final intraoperative extension angle (FIEA).
METHODS: Prospective observational cohort of 195 primary TKAs. Intraoperative 
extension deficit correction was defined as the difference between the native 
intraoperative extension angle (NIEA) and the FIEA. The relationship between 
surgical manoeuvres used to correct the extension deficit and the resulting 
intraoperative correction was analysed. Subsequently, the influence of patient 
demographics, anatomical parameters and intraoperative robotic data on 
intraoperative extension deficit correction was evaluated.
RESULTS: Planned medial and lateral extension gaps were strongly correlated with 
intraoperative extension deficit correction (medial extension gap: r = 0.62, 
95%CI: 0.52-0.70; lateral extension gap: r = 0.61 (95%CI: 0.51-0.69); both 
p < 0.001). Each additional millimetre of medial and lateral extension gap 
corresponded to a 2.5° and 1.8° greater reduction in extension deficit, 
respectively. A standardised posterior release (including posterior osteophyte 
removal and capsular detachment) was performed in all knees; in the regression 
model, the intercept was 1.6°, representing the predicted correction at zero 
planned extension-gap increase under this protocol. Posterior cruciate ligament 
excision/posterior-stabilised design was not independently associated with 
additional correction. An explanatory regression model was derived from this 
cohort to estimate intraoperative extension deficit correction: 
1.6° + 4.3° x each mm of additional extension gap (symmetrical 1-mm increase in 
both gaps). NIEA and preoperative HKA angle were significantly associated with 
FIEA.
CONCLUSIONS: Within a standardised robotic-assisted TKA protocol, including 
systematic posterior capsular release, planned widening of the medial and 
lateral extension gaps was linearly associated with intraoperative correction of 
extension deficit. Baseline NIEA and preoperative HKA influenced the final 
intraoperative extension achieved. This model may help surgeons to restore 
intraoperative full knee extension more consistently.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

title: Intermediate outcomes from the Australian Knee Osteotomy Registry reveal low rates of reoperation and conversion to total knee replacement.
authors: Vertullo C, W-Dahl A, Hoder C, Sattler L, Lewis P
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 17. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70643.
Online  ahead of print.

Intermediate outcomes from the Australian Knee Osteotomy Registry reveal low 
rates of reoperation and conversion to total knee replacement.

Vertullo C(1)(2), W-Dahl A(3), Hoder C(4), Sattler L(2), Lewis P(5).



PURPOSE: To describe contemporary knee osteotomy (KO) practice in Australia, 
determine intermediate-term rates of reoperation and conversion to total knee 
replacement (TKR) and compare the risk of subsequent TKR between 
valgus-producing tibial osteotomy and medial unicompartmental knee replacement 
(UKR) in patients younger than 55 years with osteoarthritis.
METHODS: Data from the Australian Knee Osteotomy Registry (AKOR) and the 
Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry (AOANJRR) 
were analysed from December 2016 to September 2025. Patient demographics, 
diagnosis, surgical technique, reoperation and conversion to knee replacement 
were recorded. The primary endpoint was time to conversion of the osteotomised 
knee to primary knee replacement, estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods. Age- and 
sex-adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) were calculated. Reoperation of the osteotomy 
was evaluated as a secondary outcome.
RESULTS: A total of 2563 KO procedures were reported, comprising 2047 primary 
tibial osteotomies, 447 primary femoral osteotomies and 69 reoperations. The 
mean age was 44.7 ± 10.8 years, 75.4% were male, and osteoarthritis was the 
primary diagnosis in 86.4%. Reoperation occurred in 2.7%, most commonly for 
inadequate correction (49.3%) and delayed union or non-union (27.5%). Cumulative 
conversion of valgus-producing tibial osteotomy to TKR was 1.5% (95% confidence 
interval [CI] 0.8%-2.6%) at 6 years and 2.1% (95% CI 1.2%-3.8%) at 8 years. 
Among patients younger than 55 years with osteoarthritis, medial UKR had a 
higher hazard of subsequent TKR than valgus-producing tibial osteotomy (HR 6.20, 
95% CI 3.35-11.49; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: KO was predominantly performed in relatively young, healthy 
patients and demonstrated low intermediate-term rates of reoperation and 
conversion to TKR. In patients younger than 55 years with osteoarthritis, 
valgus-producing tibial osteotomy was associated with a lower risk of subsequent 
TKR than medial UKR.

title: Kaplan fiber tenodesis and anterolateral ligament reconstruction provide comparable functional outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A propensity score-matched study at a minimum 2-year follow-up.
authors: Brossier C, Pintore A, Vermorel PH, Boyer B, Philippot R, Néri T
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 17. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70690.
Online  ahead of print.

Kaplan fiber tenodesis and anterolateral ligament reconstruction provide 
comparable functional outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: 
A propensity score-matched study at a minimum 2-year follow-up.

Brossier C(1), Pintore A(2), Vermorel PH(1), Boyer B(3), Philippot R(1), Néri 
T(4)(5).



PURPOSE: Anterolateral augmentation is widely performed alongside anterior 
cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction to reduce residual rotational laxity and 
graft failure. Two strategies coexist: anterolateral ligament reconstruction 
(ALLR), using a free tendon graft, and lateral extra-articular tenodesis using 
the iliotibial band (ITB). Kaplan fibre tenodesis (KFT) uses the native ITB to 
reconstruct the distal Kaplan fibres at their anatomical femoral footprint. The 
purpose of this study was to compare functional outcomes and graft survival 
between these two anterolateral procedures. It was hypothesized that both 
techniques would provide equivalent functional outcomes at a minimum 2-year 
follow-up.
METHODS: A retrospective comparative study was conducted using data from a 
prospective single-surgeon ACL reconstruction registry. Allocation to KFT or 
ALLR was determined intraoperatively by semitendinosus graft diameter. 
Propensity-score matching (1:1, nearest-neighbour) included age, sex, 
preoperative Tegner score, meniscal status and chondropathy, with exact matching 
on meniscal status. The primary outcome was functional outcome at a minimum 
24-month follow-up, assessed with the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome 
Score (KOOS), the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective 
score, the Tegner activity scale and the Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) 
for the IKDC, analyzed for equivalence using the two one-sided tests procedure 
with prespecified margins. Graft survival was secondary.
RESULTS: Thirty-two pairs were matched from 106 eligible patients, with adequate 
covariate balance (all standardized mean differences < 0.13). Median follow-up 
was 44 months [interquartile range = 33-47] in the KFT group and 46 months 
[35-60] in the ALLR group. No significant difference was found for KOOS global 
(84.2 vs. 85.2; p = 0.153), IKDC (85.2 vs. 82.9; p = 0.176) or Tegner (7 vs. 7; 
p = 0.941). Equivalence was demonstrated for KOOS global (+5.21, 90% confidence 
interval [CI] = [+0.63 to +9.78]; p = 0.043) and Tegner (-0.06, 90% CI = [-0.88 
to +0.76]; p = 0.031); for IKDC, the upper bound marginally exceeded the margin 
(+5.89, 90% CI = [+0.11 to +11.66]; p = 0.055). PASS-IKDC was reached by 27 of 
32 (84.4%) versus 20 of 32 (62.5%) patients (p = 0.065). Graft re-rupture 
occurred in 2 of 43 KFT patients (4.7%) and 5 of 63 ALLR patients (7.9%) 
(log-rank p = 0.879).
CONCLUSION: In patients undergoing primary ACL reconstruction, KFT provided 
functional outcomes equivalent to ALLR for the KOOS and Tegner scores at a 
minimum 2-year follow-up. Anterolateral stabilization can be achieved with an 
ITB-based technique at an anatomical femoral footprint, without a free tendon 
graft.

cohort with propensity-score matching.

title: The Influence of Peripheral Artery Disease on Postoperative Complications Following Open Reduction and Internal Fixation for Ankle Fractures.
authors: Sontam TR, Tummala S, Mittal MM, Wukich DK
abstract:

10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01630. Epub 2026 Apr 21.

The Influence of Peripheral Artery Disease on Postoperative Complications 
Following Open Reduction and Internal Fixation for Ankle Fractures.

Sontam TR(1), Tummala S, Mittal MM, Wukich DK.



BACKGROUND: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) has been associated with an 
increased risk of wound complications and surgical site infection following open 
reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) for ankle fractures. However, longer-term 
outcomes, including fracture healing, remain poorly characterized. This study 
evaluates the association between PAD and short- and long-term postoperative 
complications following ankle ORIF.
METHODS: The TriNetX Research Network was queried to identify patients who 
underwent isolated unimalleolar, bimalleolar, trimalleolar, or syndesmotic ORIF 
for ankle fractures. Patients were classified as having PAD if they had a 
documented diagnosis within 6 months before surgery, whereas patients without 
PAD served as controls. PAD and non-PAD cohorts were 1:1 propensity score 
matched for demographics and medical comorbidities. Postoperative complications 
were assessed at 90 days and 2 years.
RESULTS: After propensity matching, 2,159 patients were included in each cohort. 
At 90 days, patients with PAD had markedly higher rates of surgical site 
infection (5.5% vs 2.0%), wound disruption (10.2% vs 3.9%), lower extremity 
cellulitis (7.6% vs 2.1%), and acute osteomyelitis of the ankle or foot (3.1% vs 
0.6%) (all P < 0.001). At 2 years, PAD was associated with increased risks of 
nonunion (RR 3.07, 95% CI, 1.69 to 5.60), chronic osteomyelitis (RR 8.42, 95% 
CI, 4.64 to 15.27), implant infection (RR 3.19, 95% CI, 2.47 to 4.11), implant 
removal (RR 1.54, 95% CI, 1.32 to 1.81), and below-knee amputation (RR 10.5, 95% 
CI, 5.50 to 20.03) (all P ≤ 0.0001).
CONCLUSIONS: PAD is associated with markedly increased short- and long-term 
complications following ankle ORIF, including a sustained risk of impaired 
fracture healing. These findings underscore the importance of long-term risk 
stratification in patients with PAD undergoing ankle fracture fixation.

title: Arthroscopic technique for anterior cruciate ligament repair augmented with an internal brace: Current technique.
authors: Thilak J, Jyothish G, Cyriac M
abstract:

ahead  of print.

Arthroscopic technique for anterior cruciate ligament repair augmented with an 
internal brace: Current technique.

Thilak J(1), Jyothish G(1), Cyriac M(1).



Primary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) repair serves as a joint-preserving 
surgical option for carefully selected acute proximal ACL tears (Sherman Type I 
and II) presenting within 4 weeks of injury. The proximal ACL stump is secured 
using high-strength FiberWire sutures, which are passed through the adjustable 
loop of a cortical button incorporating a FiberTape suture that acts as an 
internal brace. The distal ends of the repair sutures and internal brace tape 
are subsequently fixed to the proximal anteromedial tibial cortex using an 
externally attachable button system. Compared with conventional ACL 
reconstruction, primary repair aims to preserve the native ACL stump and its 
proprioceptive mechanoreceptors, which may theoretically maintain dynamic 
stability and physiological knee kinematics while avoiding donor-site morbidity. 
The internal brace acts as a secondary mechanical stabilizer during the early 
healing phase, sharing loads to prevent gap formation and protect the biological 
repair during early motion. This technical note describes patient selection 
criteria, portal placement, precise construct assembly, differential 
knee-flexion tensioning, and a criteria-based postoperative rehabilitation 
protocol.

title: Nonoperative Management Deserves Consideration for Select Patients with Valgus-Impacted Femoral Neck Fractures.
authors: Bishop JA, Goodnough LH
abstract:
1. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2026 Nov 18;108(22):1753-1757. doi:
10.2106/JBJS.26.00939.  Epub 2026 Sep 22.

Nonoperative Management Deserves Consideration for Select Patients with 
Valgus-Impacted Femoral Neck Fractures.

Bishop JA(1), Goodnough LH.



The valgus-impacted femoral neck fracture is unique among hip fractures. 
Patients are often relatively comfortable, and the fracture pattern is 
inherently more stable than other femoral neck fracture types. In situ fixation 
remains the default treatment for most surgeons, and this remains a reasonable 
approach, particularly for patients unable to reliably protect their 
weight-bearing. However, multiple randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses 
have revealed that, when surgery is chosen, arthroplasty carries a lower risk of 
reoperation and implant-related complications than fixation, with no difference 
in mortality. Additionally, nonoperative management has achieved rates of 
uneventful healing comparable with those of fixation in appropriately selected 
patients who were able to protect their weight-bearing, and delayed arthroplasty 
after failed nonoperative treatment has not been associated with excess 
morbidity compared with acute arthroplasty across measured outcomes. Given that 
fixation in situ may not have dramatically better efficacy than nonoperative 
care and that failed nonoperative management can be salvaged with delayed 
arthroplasty without excess morbidity, we propose that nonoperative management 
is a reasonable initial treatment for select patients. The best candidates are 
patients who are cognitively intact, living independently, and medically stable 
and who are reasonably comfortable and capable of mobilizing while protecting 
their weight-bearing. Close clinical and radiographic follow-up is required, 
with a low threshold for conversion to arthroplasty in the setting of 
uncontrolled pain, poor mobilization, or radiographic evidence of loss of 
reduction. Dementia, high comorbidity burden, and assisted living status are 
associated with failure of nonoperative management. In all circumstances, both 
fixation and acute arthroplasty remain valid alternative strategies. We advocate 
a shared decision-making approach that accounts for the risks and benefits of 
all treatment strategies as well as patient factors.

title: Chlorhexidine Gluconate and Hypersensitivity From 2-Octyl Cyanoacrylate Mesh Dressings.
authors: Aastroem K, Ossolinski G, Silverio L, Neuwirth AL, Cooper HJ, Shah RP
abstract:

10.5435/JAAOS-D-26-00078. Epub 2026 Jul 21.

Chlorhexidine Gluconate and Hypersensitivity From 2-Octyl Cyanoacrylate Mesh 
Dressings.

Aastroem K(1), Ossolinski G, Silverio L, Neuwirth AL, Cooper HJ, Shah RP.



BACKGROUND: Both 2-octyl cyanoacrylate mesh dressings and chlorhexidine 
gluconate are independently associated with hypersensitivity. Residual 
chlorhexidine antiseptic trapped under an impermeable mesh dressing may 
synergistically contribute to skin reactions. We hypothesized that an enhanced 
washing protocol before dressing application would reduce the incidence of 
hypersensitivity. We secondarily compared delayed wound healing, infection, and 
sensitization from prior exposure with mesh dressings.
METHODS: This retrospective study reviewed 214 hip and knee arthroplasty 
patients receiving 2% chlorhexidine gluconate/70% isopropyl alcohol skin paint 
and a 2-octyl cyanoacrylate mesh dressing. The standard wash protocol (n = 138) 
informally wiped the skin prep with saline. The enhanced wash protocol (n = 76) 
thoroughly removed the skin prep with an isopropyl alcohol-soaked sponge 
followed by a saline soaked sponge. The chart was reviewed for hypersensitivity, 
wound healing, infection, and prior exposure.
RESULTS: The enhanced wash protocol was associated with a notable decrease in 
the rate of hypersensitivity from 14.5 to 2.6% (OR 0.16, 95% CI, [0.04-0.70]). 
The two reactions in the enhanced protocol occurred immediately and both 
subsequently revealed a history of adhesive allergy. More folliculitis was 
observed in the enhanced group (3.9 vs. 0%, P = 0.04). No differences were 
observed in delayed wound healing, superficial infection, or deep infection ( P 
= 0.75, 0.53, and 1, respectively). Prior mesh exposure had no effect on 
hypersensitivity.

associated with a lower incidence of hypersensitivity after application of 
impermeable mesh dressings. The study findings support efforts to reduce 
chlorhexidine concentration on the skin before the application of dressings. In 
the absence of a prospective study, we recommend making this inexpensive and 
simple protocol change before application of a 2-octyl cyanoacrylate mesh 
dressing to surgical wounds.

title: Frailty is a Vital Tool for Predicting Outcomes Following Prophylactic Femur Fixation.
authors: Sbaih O, Koltenyuk V, Gupta N, Dixon L, Gill V, Ogburn M, Williamson TK, Alderete J
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3312-e3319. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-00647. Epub 2026 Jun 23.

Frailty is a Vital Tool for Predicting Outcomes Following Prophylactic Femur 
Fixation.

Sbaih O(1), Koltenyuk V, Gupta N, Dixon L, Gill V, Ogburn M, Williamson TK, 
Alderete J.



BACKGROUND: Frailty measures have become increasingly common in the literature 
as proposed mechanisms for identifying patients at risk of adverse postoperative 
outcomes. Prophylactic femur fixation in patients with metastatic disease can 
prevent future fracture and improve quality of life; however, these patients are 
inherently high-risk surgical candidates. The role of this study is to 
characterize the relationship between frailty and postoperative outcomes in 
patients undergoing prophylactic femoral fixation (ProphFF) and compare the 
predictive ability of different frailty measures for adverse outcomes in this 
population.
METHODS: Data from the 2015 to 2020 American College of Surgeons National 
Surgical Quality Improvement Program database was used. The study focused on 
patients aged ≥18 years undergoing ProphFF and those undergoing PathFF. Frailty 
was measured using both the revised Risk Analysis Index (RAI-rev) and the 
five-factor modified Frailty Index (mFI-5). Primary outcomes included 30-day 
mortality, major complications, unplanned readmission, and unplanned revision 
surgery, nonhome discharge, and extended length of stay. Propensity score 
matching was employed to adjust for baseline differences of age, body mass 
index, sex, functional status, and ASA between ProphFF and PathFF groups. 
Statistical methods included multivariable logistic regression and receiver 
operating characteristic curve analysis to evaluate the relationships between 
frailty measures and postoperative outcomes.
RESULTS: A total of 921 patients (57.7% female, median age 65 years [IQR, 56 to 
72 years]) undergoing ProphFF or PathFF were included. Multivariable analysis 
demonstrated that increasing frailty increased odds of 30-day mortality, with 
each 1-point increase in RAI-rev and mFI-5 associated with a 5% (OR: 1.05, 95% 
CI, 1.01 to 1.08; P < 0.01) and 31% (OR: 1.31, 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.71; P < 0.05) 
higher mortality risk, respectively. Propensity score matching resulted in 842 
patients (421 prophylactic and 421 pathologic). Patients undergoing PathFF had 
higher likelihood of mortality compared with patients undergoing ProphFF (OR: 
2.79, 95% CI, 1.61 to 4.82; P < 0.01). RAI-rev (C-statistic 0.73 [95% CI, 0.71 
to 0.75]) had superior discrimination for mortality compared with mFI-5 
(C-statistic 0.57 [95% CI, 0.54 to 0.59], P < 0.001).
DISCUSSION: Increasing preoperative frailty scores, particularly as measured by 
the revised Risk Analysis Index, were independent predictors of mortality and 
morbidity in patients undergoing prophylactic femur fixation. Pathologic 
fracture fixation demonstrated higher risk of revision surgery and mortality 
compared with prophylactic fixation. These findings suggest that the RAI-rev may 
be a valuable tool for identifying high-risk patients and optimizing surgical 
candidate selection before prophylactic femur fixation, potentially improving 
outcomes in this complex patient population.

title: Immediate Weight Bearing Is Safe Following Combined Extended Trochanteric Osteotomy and Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty.

Immediate Weight Bearing Is Safe Following Combined Extended Trochanteric 
Osteotomy and Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty.

Abwini LZ(1), Tang A, Zeiman M, Andriani NT, Gillinov L, Shichman I, Schwarzkopf 
R, Liporace FA, Yoon RS.



INTRODUCTION: An extended trochanteric osteotomy (ETO) is used in complex cases 
to enhance access to the femoral canal and aid implant and cement removal during 
revision total hip arthroplasty (RTHA). However, there is no consensus regarding 
postoperative rehabilitation protocols. The aim of this study was to assess the 
efficacy and safety of immediate weight-bearing (WB) protocols in patients 
undergoing ETO during RTHA.
METHODS: A multicenter retrospective review was conducted at two academic 
medical centers between 2014 and 2021 to identify patients undergoing an ETO 
during RTHA with a minimum 1-year follow-up. Thirty-nine patients underwent an 
immediate WB protocol postoperatively. Union rates, ambulatory status, 90-day 
orthopaedic-related complications, revision surgeries, revisions, and Hip 
Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score Joint Replacement (HOOS JR) scores 
were collected.
RESULTS: Fifty-three patients were included in the final analysis. The average 
follow-up time was 15.8 ± 20.4 months, with a mean age of 63.7 ± 11.5 years. 
Bony union was achieved in 46 patients (86.8%). The mean earliest time to union 
was 4.2 ± 5.4 months. Average HOOS JR scores significantly improved from 
preoperative to 1-year follow-up (mean 16.4 ± 4.1 vs 3.5 ± 4.2), P ≤ 0.000001). 
At the final follow-up, ambulatory status improved, with fewer patients kept as 
non-weight bearing (11 (21.6%) versus 7 (15.2%)). Two complications (3.8%) due 
to deep infection, 5 revision surgeries (9.4%), and 6 revisions (11.0%) were 
observed within 90 days.
CONCLUSION: Most patients who underwent ETO during RTHA and were placed on an 
immediate WB protocol achieved union at 4.2 months on average. HOOS JR scores 
improved as early as 2 weeks. More importantly, a greater proportion of patients 
experienced an improved ambulatory status at the final follow-up. These findings 
suggest that an immediate WB protocol-particularly WBAT-may be effective and 
safely implemented in patients undergoing an ETO during RTHA.

title: Altered quadriceps forces and patellofemoral joint loading during walking in adolescents with patellar instability.
authors: Dastgerdi AK, Maine S, Saxby DJ, Carty CP
abstract:

ahead  of print.

Altered quadriceps forces and patellofemoral joint loading during walking in 
adolescents with patellar instability.

Dastgerdi AK(1), Maine S(2), Saxby DJ(1), Carty CP(3).



INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES: Patellofemoral instability is a common and clinically 
important knee disorder in children and adolescents, but its functional 
biomechanics during walking remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to 
compare gait kinematics, quadriceps muscle forces, and patellofemoral joint 
contact forces during walking between adolescents with recurrent patellar 
instability (PFP) and typically developing (TD) controls. We hypothesized that 
the PFP group would exhibit altered gait kinematics together with reduced or 
redistributed quadriceps-force and patellofemoral contact-force patterns during 
gait.
METHODS: This study used an electromyography (EMG)-informed neuromusculoskeletal 
modeling framework to compare gait kinematics, quadriceps muscle forces, and 
patellofemoral joint contact-force waveforms during walking between adolescent 
participants with PFP and TD controls. Forty-eight adolescents were included, 
comprising 24 participants with PFP and 24 controls. Three-dimensional gait 
analysis, ground reaction forces, and surface EMG were collected during level 
walking. Between-group differences were evaluated using peak comparisons, 
statistical parametric mapping (SPM), and principal component analysis (PCA).
RESULTS: No significant between-group differences were detected in kinematic 
waveforms using SPM (all p > 0.05). In contrast, significant differences were 
identified in patellofemoral joint contact-force waveforms in the mediolateral 
(cluster-level p = 0.0497 and p < 0.001) and proximodistal (both cluster-level p 
< 0.001) directions. Peak comparisons further showed larger relative differences 
in quadriceps muscle forces and patellofemoral joint contact-force components 
than in most kinematic variables. The PCA identified additional between-group 
differences in selected frontal- and transverse-plane kinematic waveforms, 
patellofemoral joint contact-force waveforms, and quadriceps force waveforms, 
particularly for vastus lateralis and rectus femoris. The PFP group also showed 
broader dispersion of principal component scores, indicating greater 
between-subject variability.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that adolescent PFP during walking is 
characterized less by large overt differences in gross gait kinematics and more 
by altered quadriceps force and patellofemoral joint loading patterns. 
EMG-informed neuromusculoskeletal modeling may therefore provide clinically 
relevant biomechanical information that could support future patient-specific 
assessment and rehabilitation research beyond conventional gait analysis alone.

and the proximal tibiofibular gap sign (PTFG-Sign) were evaluated as 
radiographic quality parameters. Reliability and rotational effects were 
analysed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), repeated-measures 
analysis of variance and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses.
RESULTS: Intra- and interrater reliability ranged from moderate to excellent 
(ICC 0.71-0.90). Medial and lateral PTS measurements at 0° and 5° of IR or ER 
did not differ significantly, whereas larger rotations produced systematic 
deviations. Medial PTS was more affected (-3.3° to +2.8°) than lateral PTS 
(-1.9° to +2.5°). ROC analyses demonstrated that fibular visibility between -5% 
and 21% relative to the posterior tibial condyles or approximately 55%-80% 
relative to the posterior tibial cortex, combined with a positive PTFG-Sign, was 
associated with neutral tibial rotation.
CONCLUSION: PTS measurements on lateral knee radiographs are rotation-dependent 
and remain accurate within approximately ±5° of tibial rotation, whereas 
rotations ≥10° result in systematic error. Tibia-based fibular parameters may 
help identify radiographs suitable for reliable PTS assessment.

title: Is There an Association Between Abnormal Patellofemoral Morphology and Patellofemoral Osteochondritis Dissecans in Pediatric Patients?
authors: Kuka CC, Syed AN, Landrum K, Mitchell BC, Sarkar S, Ganley TJ
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Nov 17:3635465261502201. doi: 10.1177/03635465261502201.
 Online ahead of print.

Is There an Association Between Abnormal Patellofemoral Morphology and 
Patellofemoral Osteochondritis Dissecans in Pediatric Patients?

Kuka CC(1), Syed AN(1), Landrum K(1), Mitchell BC(1), Sarkar S(1), Ganley TJ(1).



BACKGROUND: The cause of patellofemoral osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions 
is not clear. Biomechanical factors, such as abnormal patellofemoral morphology 
seen in patients with patellofemoral instability (PFI), may contribute to the 
development of patellofemoral OCD.
PURPOSE: To determine whether anatomic risk factors associated with PFI are also 
present in patients with patellofemoral OCD.
STUDY DESIGN: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
METHODS: The authors compared 3 groups of pediatric (≤ 19 years of age) patients 
evaluated at the study institution from 2001 to 2024: (1) those with 
patellofemoral OCD and no history of PFI, (2) those with recurrent (≥2 
dislocations) PFI with no evidence of OCD, and (3) those without known knee 
pathology (controls). Patients were propensity score matched 1:1:1 by age, sex, 
and body mass index. Measurements of patellar height, position, translocation, 
and trochlear dysplasia were collected from magnetic resonance imaging scans 
obtained before any intervention and compared between patients with 
patellofemoral OCD and PFI, and patients with patellofemoral OCD and controls. 
Statistical analysis was performed in R Version 4.3.2.
RESULTS: In total, 306 patients (102 in each group) met inclusion criteria. 
Caton-Deschamps index (CDI) and tibial tuberosity-trochlear groove (TT-TG) 
distance were significantly higher in patients with OCD compared to controls 
(CDI: 1.0 ± 0.16 for controls vs 1.1 ± 0.17 for OCD, P < .001; TT-TG: 12.9 ± 4.0 
for controls vs 14.6 ± 4.1 for OCD, P = .004). All other measures of patellar 
and trochlear dysplasia were not significantly different between controls and 
patients with OCD. All measures of patellar and trochlear morphology differed 
significantly between OCD and PFI groups, and control and PFI groups. Logistic 
regression analysis indicated increased risk of patellofemoral OCD in patients 
with an increase in CDI (OR, 1.47; P < .001) and TT-TG (OR, 1.23; P < .001).
CONCLUSION: Morphological characteristics of PFI do not appear to be associated 
with patellofemoral OCD. Rather, patients with patellofemoral OCD have knee 
anatomy that appears to be distinct from both patients with recurrent 
instability and controls with normal knee anatomy.

PMID: 43042767

title: The Open Versus Closed Access Publication Advantage in Orthopaedic Surgery.
authors: Kothari SK, Nemirov D, Shamith S, Kothari NK, Ilyas AM
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3239-e3246. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-00915. Epub 2026 May 13.

The Open Versus Closed Access Publication Advantage in Orthopaedic Surgery.

Kothari SK(1), Nemirov D, Shamith S, Kothari NK, Ilyas AM.



BACKGROUND: As scientific publishing has shifted to digital platforms, two 
primary article-publishing modalities have emerged: open access and closed 
access. Open access is freely accessible with an article processing charge (APC) 
paid by authors, whereas closed access lies behind paywalls, with low to no APC 
for authors. As the academic community increasingly relies on digital 
dissemination, it is critical to evaluate how these models influence research 
visibility and impact. This study compared open versus closed access randomized 
control trials (RCTs) across five prevalent orthopaedic conditions by analyzing 
attention scores, social media metrics, readership, and citations. The study 
hypothesis was that open access publications would have higher attention and 
readership, whereas closed access articles would yield more citations.
METHODS: A PubMed search was conducted in May 2025 to identify RCTs on rotator 
cuff tears, carpal tunnel syndrome, hip fractures, anterior cruciate ligament 
tears, and Achilles tendon ruptures. Altmetric Attention Scores, X mentions, 
Facebook mentions, news mentions, Mendeley readers, and Dimensions citations 
were collected for each article using the Altmetric Explorer database. A 
negative binomial regression, adjusted for time since publication, was used to 
compare metrics between open and closed access publications.
RESULTS: Of 1,223 articles studied, 53.8% of the articles were open access and 
46.2% were closed access. Open access articles had significantly higher 
Altmetric Attention Scores (44.1 ± 197 vs 17.2 ± 52.0), X mentions (32.2 ± 27.1 
vs 17.4 ± 38.4), Facebook mentions (1.2 ± 4.3 vs 1 ± 2.5), news mentions (4.1 ± 
25.2 vs 1.0 ± 7.2), number of Mendeley readers (136.6 ± 127.9 vs 113.4 ± 108), 
and, notably, number of Dimensions citations (36.8 ± 88.9 vs 30.1 ± 45.6) 
compared with closed access articles ( P < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Contrary to our initial hypothesis, open access articles had higher 
attention metrics and citation numbers when compared with closed access 
publications. These findings suggest that open access publishing not only 
enhances visibility and engagement but also may increase academic impact across 
multiple orthopaedic subspecialties.

title: Long-term market value decline after medial collateral ligament injury in professional football players did not differ statistically significantly from matched non-injured controls: A Transfermarkt-based cohort study.
authors: D'Ambrosi R, Mei A, Sconfienza LM, Conteduca J, Legnani C, Göktepe MC, Fink C, Baumert P
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Nov 16;21:101249. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101249. Online
ahead  of print.

Long-term market value decline after medial collateral ligament injury in 
professional football players did not differ statistically significantly from 
matched non-injured controls: A Transfermarkt-based cohort study.

D'Ambrosi R(1), Mei A(2), Sconfienza LM(3), Conteduca J(4), Legnani C(5), 
Göktepe MC(6), Fink C(7), Baumert P(8).



PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to characterize the longitudinal trajectory 
of estimated market value after medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury in 
professional football players and determine whether postinjury changes differed 
from matched non-injured controls.
METHODS: Professional football players with a recorded MCL injury were 
identified from Transfermarkt injury records labeled as medial (collateral) 
ligament injuries (seasons 2007/08-2023/24); duplicate records of the same 
episode were merged, and injuries were not clinically verified. Market value was 
assessed during the season preceding injury (Tpre), the injury season (T0), and 
annually for five subsequent seasons (T1-T5). Linear mixed-effect models 
evaluated longitudinal changes and associations with age, playing position, 
league level, and injury-related absence. Segmented models assessed changes in 
temporal trajectory. MCL cases were also matched 1:2 to non-injured controls by 
competition, season, playing position, age, and preinjury market value, with 
group differences examined using a difference-in-differences model.
RESULTS: Forty-five players with 50 MCL injury episodes were included, 8 of 
which had an associated anterior cruciate ligament or meniscal lesion. Median 
age at injury was 26.5 years (interquartile range [IQR]: 23.0-28.7), and median 
time lost was 42 days (IQR: 21-76.5). In the adjusted model, market value did 
not differ statistically significantly from Tpre at T0 (P = 0.649), T1 (P = 
0.813), or T2 (P = 0.064) but was statistically significantly lower at T3 
(-34.25%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -51.21% to -11.38%; P = 0.006), T4 
(-47.54%; 95% CI: -61.54% to -28.43%; P < 0.001), and T5 (-51.70%; 95% CI: 
-65.25% to -32.88%; P < 0.001). No statistically significant postinjury change 
in slope was observed (P = 0.103). Thirty-one of 48 eligible cases were matched 
to 62 controls; the remaining 17 had no eligible control within the matching 
criteria, mostly because of lower-tier competition or low preinjury market 
value. Difference-in-differences estimates were not statistically significant at 
any time point (P = 0.167-0.561; range: -10.9% [95% CI: -39.2% to 30.6%] at T0 
to -24.6% [95% CI: -49.5% to 12.6%] at T3); the study could detect only 
differences of approximately 42%-46% or more. Results were unchanged when 
analyses were restricted to isolated MCL injuries.
CONCLUSIONS: Market value declined substantially during long-term follow-up 
after MCL injury, but this decline was not statistically significantly different 
from that observed in matched non-injured players (P = 0.167-0.561). Much of the 
apparent long-term depreciation may therefore reflect the underlying age- and 
career-related trajectory of professional footballers; however, the matched 
analysis was underpowered, and a modest injury-specific effect, particularly 
after more severe injuries with longer absence, cannot be excluded. Because 
injury grade and treatment were unavailable, these findings should not be 
generalized to high-grade or operatively treated MCL injuries.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Does Specialty Matter? A Comparison of Early Postoperative Clinical Outcomes Following Lower Extremity Amputation Between Orthopaedic and Vascular Surgeons.
authors: Reddy S, Subramanian T, Lee W
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3342-e3358. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01375. Epub 2026 Apr 22.

Does Specialty Matter? A Comparison of Early Postoperative Clinical Outcomes 
Following Lower Extremity Amputation Between Orthopaedic and Vascular Surgeons.

Reddy S(1), Subramanian T, Lee W.



BACKGROUND: Lower extremity amputation (LEA) is performed by diverse 
specialties, including orthopaedic surgery and vascular surgery; whether 
outcomes differ by specialty remains uncertain. This study compared early 
postoperative outcomes after LEA performed by orthopaedic and vascular surgeons.
METHODS: Patients who underwent LEA surgeries were identified within the 
National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database. National Surgical 
Quality Improvement Program was queried for above-knee amputation, below-knee 
amputation, and foot amputations performed by orthopaedic or vascular surgeons. 
Patients were matched in a 1:1 ratio using propensity scores using a mixed 
exact/caliper approach. Primary outcomes were 30-day mortality, readmission, and 
revision surgery; secondary outcomes included cardiac, pulmonary, wound-related 
issues, and discharge disposition.
RESULTS: A total of 26,925 LEA cases were identified. After propensity matching, 
3,580 cases remained: orthopaedic surgery 1790 versus vascular surgery 1790, 
including 3,180 matched below-knee amputation, 806 matched above-knee 
amputation, and 334 matched foot amputations. Final cohorts had a similar 
distribution of demographic variables, indicating appropriate matching. 
Mortality of 4.0% versus 4.0%, readmission of 10.7% versus 11.7%, and revision 
surgery of 7.6 versus 8.3% were equivalent between orthopaedics and vascular 
surgery, respectively. The vascular cohort demonstrated higher rates of any 
postoperative complication: the sum of secondary outcomes (77.9% vs 70.4%; P < 
0.001), driven primarily by increased non-home discharge (69.7% vs 60.8%) and 
transfusion within 72 hours (19.5% vs 16.3%). When non-home discharge was 
removed, there was no difference in early postoperative complication (32.2% vs 
35.5%; P = 0.382). By contrast, the orthopaedic group had slightly higher rates 
of organ/space infection (4.1% vs 2.2%; P = 0.001) and postoperative pneumonia 
(3.8% vs 2.5%; P = 0.029), consistent with the higher proportion of 
contaminated/dirty wounds: 44.4% versus 36.0% and longer surgical duration: 79.5 
± 43.5 versus 68.3 ± 46.1 observed in this group.
CONCLUSIONS: The present analysis represents the first matched comparison of LEA 
outcomes by surgical specialty. When baseline patient risk is balanced, 
orthopaedic and vascular surgeons achieve comparable 30-day major outcomes: 
mortality, readmission, and revision surgery following LEA. Residual differences 
in complication profiles appear driven by clinical context, such as wound class, 
transfusion exposure, and rehabilitation needs, rather than by specialty itself.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Where does your allograft tissue come from? Allograft use in reconstructive orthopaedic surgery: A review of the NHSBT provision of musculoskeletal allografts in the UK.
authors: Telford J, Cornish E, Spalding T, Barkatali B
abstract:

Where does your allograft tissue come from? Allograft use in reconstructive 
orthopaedic surgery: A review of the NHSBT provision of musculoskeletal 
allografts in the UK.

Telford J(1), Cornish E(2), Spalding T(3), Barkatali B(4).



The use of musculoskeletal (MSK) allografting techniques in reconstructive 
surgery of the knee is well established, with the most common application being 
in revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. However, the journey from 
donor to recipient is poorly understood by orthopaedic surgeons. NHSBT Tissue 
Service in Liverpool is one of the largest tissue banks in Europe and provides 
MSK allograft tissue to hospitals in the UK, though it is not the sole provider. 
All stages of the process, from donor identification to distribution are tightly 
regulated by the Human Tissue Act 2004 to provide MSK allografts which retain 
the biomechanical properties required, whilst also being at an extremely low 
risk of disease transmission. This is achieved through a rigorous donor 
selection process and protocols for the harvesting, shaping, preservation, 
decontamination, sterilisation, packaging and storage of tissues This review 
describes NHSBT protocols for MSK allograft provision attained via publicly 
available data, correspondence with NHSBT staff and a tour of the facility in 
Speke, Liverpool. In addition, a review of the literature was performed to 
establish international practice, and the effect methods of retrieval, 
processing and storage can have on disease transmission and biomechanical 
properties. This review describes the production of MSK allografts by NHSBT in 
the UK.
